'''''Leersia oryzoides''''' is a species of [[Poaceae|grass]] known by the common name '''rice cutgrass'''<ref name="PearsallPiperno1995">{{cite journal|last1=Pearsall|first1=Deborah M.|last2=Piperno|first2=Dolores R.|last3=Dinan|first3=Elizabeth H.|last4=Umlauf|first4=Marcelle|last5=Zhao|first5=Zhuun|last6=Benfer|first6=Robert A.|title=Distinguishing rice (Oryza sativa Poaceae) from wild Oryza species through Phytolith analysis: Results of preliminary research|journal=Economic Botany|volume=49|issue=2|year=1995|pages=183–196|issn=0013-0001|doi=10.1007/BF02862923|bibcode=1995EcBot..49..183P |s2cid=21128182}}</ref> or just '''cut-grass'''.<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> It is a widespread grass native to Europe, Asia, and North America and present in many other regions, such as Australia, as an [[introduced species]]. This is a [[rhizome|rhizomatous]] perennial grass growing to a maximum height between 1 and 1.5 meters. The leaves are up to about 28 centimeters long and have very rough, minutely toothed edges which are sharp enough to cut skin<ref>{{Cite web |title=Leersia oryzoides (rice cut grass): Go Botany |url=https://gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org/species/leersia/oryzoides/ |access-date=2026-09-07 |website=gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org}}</ref>. The [[inflorescence]] is a loose, open array of wavy, hairlike branches bearing rows of spikelets. Each spikelet is a flat fruit with a rough, bristly [[lemma (botany)|lemma]] without an [[awn (botany)|awn]], and no [[chaff|glumes]]. Some of the spikelet branches develop within the sheaths of the leaves and are [[cleistogamy|cleistogamous]]. This grass is sometimes used for [[erosion]] control and restoring [[wetland]]s.
